problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L{y(t)}$ for $s>2$ if 

$$
{y}^{′}-2y=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(0)=1.
$$

You may make use of the following result:

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0.
$$

feedback.problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L{y(t)}$ for $s>2$ if 

$$
{y}^{′}-2y=5-2{e}^{-t},\,y(0)=\frac{1}{3}.
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}-2y} & =L{5-2{e}^{-t}} \\ L{{y}^{′}}-2L{y} & =5L{1}-2L{{e}^{-t}}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L{{y}^{′}},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=\frac{1}{3}:$

$$
L{{y}^{′}}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)-\frac{1}{3}
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}},\,s>0,\,n\in {N}_{0} \\ L{{e}^{at}} & =\frac{1}{s-a},\,s>a\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following results:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{1} & =\frac{1}{s} \\ L{{e}^{-t}} & =\frac{1}{s-(-1)}=\frac{1}{s+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}}-2L{y} & =5L{1}-2L{{e}^{-t}} \\ (sY(s)-\frac{1}{3})-2Y(s) & =\frac{5}{s}-\frac{2}{s+1} \\ (s-2)Y(s) & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{5}{s}-\frac{2}{s+1} \\ (s-2)Y(s) & =\frac{s(s+1)+15(s+1)-6s}{3s(s+1)} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}+10s+15}{3s(s+1)(s-2)}\end{aligned}
$$
